chapters.title: Chapter 3: How Property Makes and Loses Money

lessons.title: Illiquidity, Concentration and the Risks Nobody Advertises

children.text: Vivek, 45, is a senior manager at a tech company in Bengaluru. On paper he is worth ₹2.4 crore, and ₹1.8 crore of that is two flats in Bellandur. His daughter gets into a university abroad and he needs ₹25 lakh within 60 days. He cannot sell a quarter of a flat. A full sale could take months, and a buyer who knows he is in a hurry will offer less. None of this showed up in any brochure, price chart or broker's pitch. This lesson covers the risks of property that nobody advertises.

body.text: Property's biggest risks do not show up in its price: you cannot sell part of it, you cannot sell it quickly, and it often ties your wealth to the same city and industry as your salary.

children.text: Risk 1: Illiquidity

markDefs.definition: The difficulty of converting an asset into cash quickly without accepting a lower price.
A trade settles one business day after it is executed. Indian equity markets moved fully to T+1 settlement in 2023.

children.text: Sell Nifty 50 index fund units on Zerodha Coin and the money typically reaches your bank within a few business days. Sell shares on NSE and trades settle on
. Selling a flat is a completely different process, and every step adds weeks. That is
illiquidity

body.label: Typical time to sell a resale flat in India
body.context: From listing to registration, when title and documents are clean. Non-resident sellers often take 4 to 12 months because of extra tax and banking compliance. A slow market, a high asking price or a title problem can stretch this much further.

markDefs.definition: A sale made under time pressure, usually at a price below what a patient seller would get.

children.text: Illiquidity has a price, and you pay it at the worst possible moment. A seller who must close in 45 days usually has to accept a
distressed sale
discount. On a ₹1.2 crore flat, accepting 8% less to close fast costs ₹9.6 lakh, more than a year's rent many times over.

body.title: The price of hurrying
body.prompt: Kavya needs to sell her ₹90 lakh flat in Kondhwa, Pune within six weeks to fund a medical emergency. The best quick offer is 7% below fair value. How much does the rush cost her, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: ₹90 lakh × 7% = ₹6.3 lakh. That loss comes on top of brokerage and any capital gains tax. An emergency fund in liquid assets would have let her wait for a fair price, or avoid selling at all.

children.text: Risk 2: You Cannot Sell a Slice

markDefs.definition: A loan secured against a property you already own. It usually carries a higher interest rate than a home loan and puts the property at risk if you default.

children.text: If Vivek needed ₹25 lakh from a ₹1 crore mutual fund portfolio, he would redeem a quarter of it and keep the rest invested. With property, it is all or nothing. The only way to raise part of the value without selling is a
loan against property
, which means paying interest to access your own wealth, and pledging the asset in the process.

body.title: Settlement speed
body.textWithBlank: Equity trades on NSE and BSE settle on T+___, meaning one business day after the trade.
body.explanation: T+1 settlement means your sale proceeds from shares reach your broker account the next business day. A flat can take months to convert into cash.

children.text: Risk 3: Concentration

markDefs.definition: Holding a large share of your wealth in a single asset, sector or location, so one bad outcome can damage your whole financial position.

children.text: Recall the RBI finding from Chapter 1: the average Indian household held about 77% of its assets in real estate. That is extreme
concentration risk
. No professional fund manager would put three-quarters of a portfolio into one or two stocks, yet millions of families do exactly that with property.

body.latex: \text{Real Estate Concentration} = \frac{\text{Value of All Property Held}}{\text{Total Net Worth}} \times 100
body.caption: Use current market values and subtract outstanding loans from net worth. Include your own home: it is still your money locked in one asset.

children.text: 75% of Vivek's net worth sits in two flats in a single micro-market. Worse, the risk is doubled up. His salary depends on Bengaluru's tech industry. His flats' rents and resale prices also depend on Bengaluru's tech industry. A severe tech slowdown could cut his income, empty his flats of tenants and weaken buyer demand, all at the same time.

columns.label: Property-heavy household
points: One or two assets in one city decide most of the family's wealth
Job, rent and property prices often depend on the same local economy
Raising cash means selling a whole asset, slowly
A single legal, tenant or flood problem hits a large share of net worth

columns.label: Diversified household
points: Wealth spread across equity, debt, gold and property
Different assets react differently to the same event
Cash can be raised in days from liquid holdings
No single mishap can derail long-term goals

body.title: Measure the concentration
body.prompt: Farah in Hyderabad owns a flat worth ₹1.1 crore, a plot worth ₹40 lakh, equity mutual funds worth ₹30 lakh, gold worth ₹10 lakh and FDs of ₹20 lakh. She has no loans. What percentage of her net worth is in real estate? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Real estate: ₹1.1 crore + ₹40 lakh = ₹1.5 crore. Net worth: ₹1.5 crore + ₹30 lakh + ₹10 lakh + ₹20 lakh = ₹2.1 crore. Concentration: ₹1.5 crore ÷ ₹2.1 crore = 71.4%. Nearly three-quarters of her wealth is in two illiquid assets.

children.text: Risk 4: Tenants

markDefs.definition: A central template law released in 2021 for states to adopt, setting up rent authorities and courts for faster, more balanced landlord-tenant dispute resolution.

children.text: Rental income depends on a stranger paying on time and leaving when asked. When a tenant stops paying or refuses to vacate, removing them through older state rent control laws and civil courts can take years. That is why Indian landlords prefer 11-month agreements, large deposits and police verification. The
Model Tenancy Act, 2021
was designed to fix this with dedicated rent authorities and time-bound dispute resolution, but it is only a template. Each state must pass its own law, and adoption has been slow.

body.text: Reduce tenant risk before it starts: use a written, registered rental agreement, complete police verification, collect a reasonable security deposit, document the flat's condition with dated photos, and check your state's rent law. A single bad tenancy can wipe out years of rental return in lost rent, repairs and legal fees.

children.text: Risk 5: Physical and Location Risk

In September 2022, extremely heavy overnight rain flooded parts of Bengaluru's Outer Ring Road. Residents of upscale villa communities in Yemalur, including Epsilon, were evacuated on tractors and boats as water filled their homes and basements. These were some of the most expensive homes in the city. A premium price does not protect a property from a low-lying site, a blocked storm-water drain or a nearby lake overflowing.

body.text: The demolition cases carry a hard lesson: a buyer can pay in full, hold registered papers and still lose the home if the building itself was illegal. Approvals, not the sale deed alone, decide whether a building can stand. Chapter 4 shows you how to check them.

body.title: Tackling concentration
body.question: Vivek wants to reduce his concentration risk without taking on new risks. Which step helps most?
options: Buy a third flat in Bellandur to spread rent across more units
Take a loan against one flat and invest it in a plot outside the city
Direct new monthly savings into diversified mutual funds, and gradually sell one flat when the market is favourable
Move all his mutual funds into a fixed deposit
body.explanation: A third flat or a plot adds more property risk, and borrowing adds leverage. Moving funds to an FD changes nothing about property concentration. Directing savings into diversified assets, and selling one flat patiently rather than in a hurry, steadily reduces concentration.

body.title: Vivek's ₹25 lakh problem
body.scenario: Vivek has ₹1.8 crore in two Bellandur flats, ₹35 lakh in mutual funds, ₹20 lakh in EPF and ₹5 lakh in FDs. He needs ₹25 lakh within 60 days for his daughter's university fees abroad. A broker says he can sell one flat "in a month" if Vivek drops the price by 10%.
body.prompt: What are Vivek's options, and what does this episode reveal about his portfolio?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The fast route: his mutual funds and FDs total ₹40 lakh, so he can raise ₹25 lakh within days without selling property. But it uses up most of his only diversified, liquid savings, pushing property to about ₹1.8 crore ÷ ₹2.15 crore, or roughly 84% of net worth.
2. The rushed sale: a 10% discount on a flat worth roughly ₹90 lakh costs about ₹9 lakh, plus brokerage and possible capital gains tax. It raises far more cash than he needs, and still may not close in 60 days.
3. A loan against property: possible, but it adds interest cost and debt at a stressful time.
4. EPF: partial withdrawals are allowed only for specific purposes and conditions, so it is not a reliable source for this need.
5. The real lesson: his wealth looked large but was mostly locked up. He needed a planned education fund in liquid assets years earlier.
6. Going forward: rebuild liquid savings first, then reduce concentration patiently by selling one flat when market conditions and his timeline are favourable, not when he is forced to.

body.title: Stress-Test Your Property Holdings
steps: Calculate real estate as a percentage of your net worth
Keep at least 6 months of expenses in liquid assets outside property
List every big goal in the next 5 years and check it is not funded only by property
Ask whether your job and your investment property depend on the same local economy
Check flood history, drainage and building approvals for each property
Confirm every tenancy has a registered agreement and a verified tenant
Estimate how long each property would realistically take to sell, and at what discount if rushed

points: A resale flat typically takes about 2 to 6 months to sell, and rushing usually means accepting a lower price.
Property cannot be sold in parts; raising part of its value means a full sale or a loan against it.
Indian households are heavily concentrated in real estate, and job correlation can double that risk.
Tenant disputes can be slow to resolve, and the Model Tenancy Act has been adopted by only a few states.
Floods, illegal construction and demolition orders show that price, papers and prestige do not remove physical or legal risk.
Keep liquid savings outside property, cap your property concentration, and check approvals, drainage and tenancy paperwork.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. Sale timelines, tenancy laws and risks vary by state, city and property, and the examples use illustrative figures. Consult a qualified property lawyer and a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
